title: A Chunky Sea Animal From the Age of Dinosaurs
paragraphs: Sometimes the most startling discoveries come not from the field but from the storeroom. A belemnite fossil, long overlooked in a museum drawer, has now been recognised as a new species, Wyoteuthis linsterorum, in a study in Papers in Palaeontology by researchers from the United States, the United Kingdom and New Zealand.

Belemnites, extinct cousins of squid and octopuses, were abundant in the Late Jurassic inland sea that once lay over Wyoming, and the typical specimen there is a modest affair: an internal guard five to ten centimetres long and a mere one or two across. This animal broke the mould. Its guard measures about ten centimetres by six, the thickest of its kind known, and the researchers estimate the whole creature, arms included, stretched to some sixty centimetres. CT scanning tied it to a family that palaeontologists had assumed was long gone, which makes it a relict, a straggler from an older chapter of the group’s history.

The explanations on offer are, rightly, hedged. “A possible explanation is that their relatively large size gave them an advantage when hunting co-occurring smaller belemnites,” lead author Alexey Ippolitov said, and co-author Dean Lomax has floated narrow specialisation as a reason for its scarcity. Yet with just two specimens, found in the late 1990s and donated in 2019, such notions remain hypotheses. The fossils are a reminder that a species can be named on thin evidence and still be, in the best sense, a find.

questions.q: Where did the key discovery come from?
questions.a: From a fossil long overlooked in a museum drawer.

questions.q: Why is the animal called a relict?
questions.a: It belongs to a family thought to have died out long before.

questions.q: Why are the explanations called hypotheses?
questions.a: They rest on only two specimens and have not been tested.
